A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AgentSquare study. Their complete main texts and appendices provide readable, matchable methods, equations, tables, figures, and module examples; pagination and relocation do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original AgentSquare evaluations on six benchmarks, component ablations, search trajectories, API costs, and performance-predictor validation in Section 4 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds ADAS comparison results and predictor validation on dynamically searched agents.

M1.justification: The four-module workflow, module evolution, recombination, and performance predictor remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 moves to the appendix without procedural changes, and the discovered-module code examples are retained. The added ADAS and FunSearch discussion supplies attribution rather than a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WebShop, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, M3ToolEval, TravelPlanner, and PDDL with the same task coverage. The additional predictor analysis changes which agent configurations are examined within this coverage, rather than adding a dataset or task.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and A.3 add ADAS across all six benchmarks with both GPT-4o and GPT-3.5. This introduces a directly relevant whole-agent code-search comparison family beyond the previous human-designed, module-search, and prompt-search baselines. All earlier comparators remain.

E3.justification: The added predictor experiment uses dynamically searched agents as evaluation inputs, introducing an additional agent-selection procedure in Figure A.15. Existing benchmark metrics, LLM backbones, and the stopping rule of five consecutive iterations without improvement remain unchanged. Newly disclosed budget controls do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure A.15 extends predictor validation to agents generated during search, examining reliability under its intended usage conditions. Figure 5, the component ablations in Tables 2 and A.5, and the discovered-module case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional predictor scatter plots continue the existing reporting practice without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds ADAS scores and dynamically searched-agent predictor results. ADAS becomes the strongest search baseline on GPT-4o SciWorld at 0.754, above Bayesian search at 0.749; AgentSquare remains at 0.781. Previously reported benchmark and ablation scores are unchanged. Table A.6 revises six termination-iteration totals, including GPT-4o WebShop from 15 to 18 and ALFWorld from 18 to 15, without establishing reruns.

T1.justification: The module definitions, MoLAS optimization objective, and mathematical formulations in Equations 1–4 are unchanged. Neither version contains additional theorems or proofs; the new background and motivation are conceptual explanations.

C1.justification: The introduction now explicitly characterizes MoLAS as a constrained subset of ADAS's broader code-search problem, qualifying the novelty framing around modular reuse. The central modular-design, search-framework, interpretable-insight, and 17.2% average performance-gain claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 newly qualifies the comparison by explaining that ADAS could discover more sophisticated agents with additional iterations and token usage. Section 3.5 also emphasizes a more focused search space and reuse of successful module designs as explanations for AgentSquare's effectiveness.

D1.justification: Section 3.5 newly discloses reuse of ADAS implementation code, and Appendix A.1 describes adapting the official ADAS code for the benchmark comparison. Sections 4.2–4.3 newly document claimed token-budget/iteration matching and random-combination sampling for Figure 5. These disclosures do not establish changes to the existing AgentSquare implementation.

R1.justification: v2 briefly grouped ADAS with workflow-search approaches criticized as oversimplifying agents. v3 substantially repositions ADAS as a direct precursor, identifies MoLAS as a subset of its search space, acknowledges code reuse, and attributes the evolution pipeline to FunSearch. New Section 2.1 also expands the optimization background with references including Evolution through Large Models and LLMatic.

P1.justification: v3 introduces Background and Workflow Overview subsections, expands selected introduction and method passages, rewrites portions of related work, and shortens the conclusion. These are localized structural and prose revisions; most of the document remains intact.

P2.justification: Algorithm 1 moves from the main text to the appendix; Tables 1 and A.3 gain an ADAS row; and Figure A.15 is added. Several figures are resized, Figure 1's caption is shortened, and appendix displays are redistributed. Existing module examples are retained and renumbered from A.15–A.20 to A.16–A.21.

improvement.justification: v3 provides a more relevant comparison through ADAS, clearer attribution of implementation and conceptual antecedents, and additional predictor validation during search. These improve the paper's grounding while leaving its method and most evidence unchanged. A small reporting problem offsets part of the gain: Section 4.2 retains the 11.0% SciWorld improvement over search baselines, although the added ADAS result reduces the average calculated from Tables 1 and A.3 to approximately 10.6%.
